title: Why Silent Modeling Is A Powerful Strategy
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that most teachers undercut their modeling by talking too much, glossing over details, and rushing through steps, and proposes silent modeling as a fix. He lists six specific benefits: it makes the teacher more visually interesting and demonstrative, purifies instruction by removing the risk of confusing wording, narrows students' focus to a single sense so attention is easier to sustain, creates a vivid mental 'movie' students can replay, gives all students—including language learners—equal direct access to instruction, and measurably improves subsequent student performance. He is careful to note that silent modeling isn't meant to replace verbal explanation entirely but should be used deliberately alongside it. The article closes by suggesting that practicing silent modeling actually trains teachers to speak more precisely and purposefully when words are used.
points: Silent modeling forces more expressive, demonstrative body language, making instruction more engaging to watch.
Removing words from modeling purifies instruction, eliminating the risk that wording confuses or distracts students.
Narrowing attention to a single visual channel makes sustained focus easier for students.
Silent modeling gives all students, including English language learners, equal direct access to the same instruction.
Silent modeling is a complement to—not a replacement for—verbal explanation, and it trains teachers to speak more precisely when words are used.
quotes: Done right, modeling has the power to teach your students virtually anything you want them to be able to do.
One sure way to avoid these mistakes, while at the same time ensuring excellent instruction, is to model in silence.
When you take away your ability to talk, you naturally become more demonstrative and therefore more interesting to your students.
When you model in silence, you’re assured of providing the purest form of instruction.

When you model in a silent but highly detailed way—as if you’re an actual student completing the precise steps you want them to take—they will see themselves in their mind’s eye successfully doing the same, which then sticks in their memory.
When you model wordlessly, all students—including second language learners—have direct access to your best instruction.
The best feature of silent modeling is that it improves performance.
